questions.question: The price of chicken rises sharply after a bird-flu outbreak. Describe, in words, what happens in the beef market and in the charcoal market if braai packs containing chicken become more expensive — naming the relationship in each case and the direction each demand curve moves.
questions.expected_answer: Beef is a substitute for chicken: shoppers comparing relative prices swing toward beef, so at every beef price more is demanded — beef's entire demand curve shifts right (a shift, not a movement along, because beef's own price did not cause it), raising beef's equilibrium price and quantity. Charcoal is a complement of braai packs: dearer braai packs mean fewer braais, so demand for charcoal falls at every price — charcoal's demand curve shifts left. Rule: substitutes move together with the related good's price; complements move opposite.

questions.question: Define derived demand and trace both directions of the loop between product and factor markets using a housing boom as the example.
questions.expected_answer: Derived demand is demand for a factor of production that comes second-hand from demand for the product it helps make — bricklayers are demanded because houses are demanded. Forward direction: a housing boom raises house prices and building activity, which raises demand for bricklayers, cement and finance, bidding up wages and factor prices. Backward direction: those higher wages and material costs are production costs, shifting housing supply left and pushing product prices higher; and via the circular flow, higher factor incomes return as household spending in product markets.

questions.question: Name the four market structures, give one South African example of each, and state which are perfect and which imperfect markets, with the reason.
questions.expected_answer: Perfect competition — very many sellers, identical products, free entry, price takers (fresh produce markets come close). Monopolistic competition — many sellers, differentiated products, easy entry (takeaways, salons). Oligopoly — a few large interdependent firms, difficult entry (banks, mobile networks; collusion like the bread price-fixing case is illegal). Monopoly — one seller, no close substitute, blocked entry (Eskom's transmission grid), a price maker. Only perfect competition is a perfect market; the other three are imperfect because sellers hold some power over price.
